rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls human creation from nonexistence and death, then points to people whose decline makes them an example of divine power.
rows.anchor: هذا تنبيه على الاعتبار في إيجادنا بعد العدم وإماتتنا بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Old age is the final stage, when senses fail and speech falters; it is called the lowest age despite infancy sharing such dependence, because infancy begins life with strong hope.
rows.anchor: وأرذل العمر آخره الذي تفسد فيه الحواس ويختل النطق،

rows.speaker: علي رضي الله عنه
rows.claim: A view transmitted from Ali places the beginning of the lowest age at seventy-five, a common pattern rather than a fixed limit.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الناس: أول أرذل العمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no fixed age for this decline: one person may be decrepit at fifty while another at ninety is not.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا ينحصر إلى مدة معينة وإنما هو بحسب إنسان إنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose-like lam describes an outcome: a person's knowledge dwindles after once knowing things, without implying that all knowledge literally disappears.
rows.anchor: ليصير أمره بعد العلم بالأشياء إلى أن لا يعلم شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge and power do not change under events or time.
rows.anchor: علمه وقدرته التي لا تتبدل ولا تحملها الحوادث ولا تتغير

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: The unequal shares of provision establish a parable: favored humans do not make their dependents equal partners in their wealth, so how can pagans assign God's creatures a share in divinity?
rows.anchor: هذا تأويل الطبري، وحكاه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is cited for the parable that human owners do not equalize their own provision with those under their authority; the analogy rebukes associating creatures with God.
rows.anchor: وحكاه عن ابن عباس وحكي عنه أن الآية مشيرة إلى عيسى ابن مريم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says the verse alludes to Jesus son of Mary.
rows.anchor: وحكي عنه أن الآية مشيرة إلى عيسى ابن مريم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most interpreters take the command about near kin as a general charge to maintain relatives, addressed to the Prophet but applying to the community, including material and other aid when needed.
rows.anchor: فقال الجمهور: الآية وصية للناس كلهم

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: Ali ibn al-Husayn identifies the near kin as the Prophet's relatives, whose rights the Prophet was to pay from the public treasury.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن الحسين في هذه: هم قرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general interpretation is clearer because the near kin are paired with the poor and traveler.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أبين، ويعضده العطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The traveler in this verse includes rich and poor, each with a due right; the alms-tax verse uses the term more narrowly.
rows.anchor: وابن السبيل هنا يعم الغني والفقير إذ لكل واحد منهما حق وإن اختلفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waste means spending on wrongdoing or extravagantly even on permissible things; the word evokes scattering seed.
rows.anchor: «التبذير» إنفاق المال في فساد أو في سرف في مباح

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash reports that 'the squanderers' may specifically mean people of Mecca, though it may instead be a generic class.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل قوله تعالى: المبذرين أن يكون اسم جنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Squanderers are called Satan's brothers by likeness of conduct, since both pursue corruption; the word for brothers here need not mean kinship.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: إخوان يعني أنهم في حكمهم، إذ المبذر ساع في فساد

rows.speaker: الحسن والضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read 'brothers of Satan' in the singular, as does Anas ibn Malik's codex.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والضحاك «إخوان الشيطان» على الإفراد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of Satan's disbelief completes the warning against imitating his corruption.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر تعالى كفر الشيطان ليقع التحذير من التشبه به في الإفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers back to the poor and travelers; if the Prophet lacked anything to give, he should decline gently and reassure them while awaiting provision.
rows.anchor: الضمير في عنهم عائد على من تقدم ذكره من المساكين وبني السبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A gracious answer promises God's favor, offers kind reassurance and a hopeful appointment, and prays for God's generous provision.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي فيه الترجية بفضل الله تعالى والتأنيس بالميعاد الحسن والدعاء في توسعة الله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says that when he had nothing to give, the Prophet would pray that God provide from His bounty for both parties.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه عليه السلام كان يقول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ikrima interpret the hoped-for mercy as provision expected from God.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the mercy is reward: the verse concerned people whose corrupt spending made the Prophet withhold money, so God ordered a prayer for their opening and reform.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد «الرحمة» الأجر والثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports describe the youths as sons of nobles in the city of the unbelieving king Daqiyus, also called Daqliyus or Daqinus; they were Romans and followers of Jesus, though another view places them before Jesus.
rows.anchor: الفتية فيما روي، قوم من أبناء أشراف مدينة دقيوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths' foreign names have weak transmission; al-Tabari's list gives Makselminya, Majseliniya, Tamlikha, Martus, Kashutunus, Birunus, Dinamus, and Yatūnus.
rows.anchor: وأما أسماؤهم فهي أعجمية،

rows.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: In one account the youths lived under an idol-worshipping king; after learning belief from a grammarian or earlier believers, they rejected idolatry, were summoned and threatened with death, and answered with the words later quoted in 18:14-16.
rows.anchor: روى مجاهد عن ابن عباس أن هؤلاء الفتية كانوا في دين ملك يعبد الأصنام ويذبح لها ويكفر بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In one version the king delayed punishment, then the youths secretly planned to flee to a cave known to one of them.
rows.anchor: فاذهبوا إلى منازلكم ودبروا رأيكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says they hid their escape by playing with a polo mallet and ball as they moved toward the cave; another says they escaped while being taken to a festival.
rows.anchor: فخرجوا فيما روي يلعبون بالصولجان والكرة وهم يدحرجونها إلى نحو طريقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A separate account says the youths saw their city's festival idolatry, believed, and left the people to avoid sharing their punishment.
rows.anchor: فرأى الفتيان ما يمتثله الناس في ذلك العيد من الكفر وعبادة الأصنام والذبح لها

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb's account has a disciple of Jesus work in a bathhouse, convert the city's noble youths, then flee with them after the prince and a prostitute died there and the disciple was blamed.
rows.anchor: وروى وهب بن منبه أن أمرهم إنما كان أن حواريا لعيسى ابن مريم،

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says the noble youths became believers one by one, met by chance beneath a tree, learned that their aims matched, and then fled together after confiding in pairs.
rows.anchor: وقال عبيد بن عمير: إن أصحاب الكهف كانوا فتية أبناء العظماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts say the dog belonged to a youth who hunted, or that a shepherd and his dog joined the group; its name is given as Himran or Qitmir.
rows.anchor: وأما الكلب فروي أنه كان كلب صيد لبعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says God caused the youths to sleep as soon as they entered the cave, concealing their whereabouts from the kingdom.
rows.anchor: فروت فرقة أن الله عز وجل «ضرب على آذانهم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People recorded the youths' names, fathers, rank, and disappearance on lead or copper tablets; some say two secretly believing judges hid them, either at their homes or in the king's construction over the cave.
rows.anchor: من رصاص أو نحاس، وجعلوه على باب المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says the king's searchers found the cave and advised sealing it so hunger and thirst would kill the youths; God had already put them to sleep for their protection.
rows.anchor: فأمر بالدخول عليهم فهاب الرجال ذلك، فقال له بعض وزرائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The persecuting king is also said to have been a Roman ruler who sought to abolish the religion of Jesus and killed believers publicly.
rows.anchor: وكان يريد أن يذهب فيما ذكر، دين عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths sought God's mercy, interpreted by commentators as provision, and a good way out of their situation; the author says this was a worldly prayer, while they trusted their afterlife outcome.
rows.anchor: دعوا الله تعالى بأن يؤتيهم من عنده رحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read rashadan with both vowels open; Abu Raja reads rushdan with a rounded first vowel and silent second, while the majority reading better matches surrounding verse endings.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «رشدا» بفتح الراء والشين، وقرأ أبو رجاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words may also include mercy in the afterlife, and the author recommends this verse as a sufficient prayer for a believer's worldly needs.
rows.anchor: وينبغي لكل مؤمن أن يجعل دعاءه في أمر دنياه هذه الآية فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Striking over the ears expresses imposing sleep with force and close adherence; Arabic uses the same image for imposed humiliation, taxation, or military levies.
rows.anchor: ويعبر عن هذا ونحوه ب «الضرب» لتبين قوة المباشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line attributed to al-Farazdaq demonstrates the expression's sense of something firmly imposed or enveloping.
rows.anchor: ضربت عليك العنكبوت بنسجها ...

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ear is singled out because sleep strongly affects hearing and sleepers commonly wake through the ear; a Prophetic report describes Satan urinating in the ear of one who sleeps through the night.
rows.anchor: الجارحة التي منها عظم فساد النوم، وقلما ينقطع نوم نائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective 'counted' describes the years to intensify their number; al-Zajjaj also allows it as a cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: وقوله عددا نعت للسنين، والقصد به العبارة عن التكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To raise or send forth means to set in motion after stillness, whether a person was physically still or merely inactive in the relevant matter.
rows.anchor: و «البعث» التحريك بعد سكون، وهذا مطرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'So that We might know' means bringing the matter into existence, not acquiring knowledge, since God already knew which group best reckoned the duration; al-Zuhri reads the verb with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهذا على نحو كلام العرب أي لنعلم ذلك موجودا، وإلا

rows.speaker: الجمهور من المفسرين
rows.claim: The apparent two groups are the youths, who thought they had slept briefly, and the townspeople alive when they awoke, who had preserved a record of them.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الجمهور من المفسرين، وقالت فرقة: هما حزبان من الكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify the two groups as believers, but the author says that reading does not fit the verse's wording.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: هما حزبان من المؤمنين، وهذا لا يرتبط من ألفاظ الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes ahsā as a past-tense verb with amad as its object; al-Zajjaj instead analyzes ahsā as a superlative and amad as specification, a construction the author says is unusual for a quadriliteral verb.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله أحصى فالظاهر الجيد فيه أنه فعل ماض

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj analyzes ahsā as a superlative and amad as an accusative of specification; the author notes examples that support such superlatives from quadriliteral verbs.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أحصى هو أفعل، وأمدا على هذا نصب على التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amad means an endpoint and can refer to a duration because a duration has a limit.
rows.anchor: و «الأمد» الغاية، وتأتي عبارة عن المدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amad is glossed as a number, an approximate explanation by meaning, following the Mujahid attribution at the preceding segment boundary.
rows.anchor: أمدا معناه عددا، وهذا تفسير بالمعنى على جهة التقريب

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari makes amad the object of labithu, a grammatical analysis the author rejects as untenable.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: نصب أمدا ب لبثوا، وهذا غير متجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the dispute over which group best counted the duration, God says that He recounts their true story; these verses answer Quraysh's questions prompted by the Israelites.
rows.anchor: لما اقتضى قوله لنعلم أي الحزبين أحصى [الكهف: 12]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qass means reporting a connected, unfolding account, rather than reproducing a conversation word for word.
rows.anchor: و «القص» الإخبار بأمر يسرد، لا بكلام يروى شيئا شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Increasing their guidance means enabling righteous action, devotion, separation from people, and renunciation of worldly life, additions to their faith.
rows.anchor: وزدناهم هدى أي يسرناهم للعمل الصالح والانقطاع إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tying their hearts is a metaphor for the resolve and patience God gave them; firmness is pictured as binding what fear might loosen.
rows.anchor: وربطنا على قلوبهم عبارة عن شدة عزم وقوة صبر أعطاها الله لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their standing and speaking may describe their courageous appearance before the unbelieving king, when they rejected his religion despite threats.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أن يكون هذا وصف مقامهم بين يدي الملك الكافر، فإنه مقام يحتاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, standing means resolving firmly to flee to God and oppose their people; this better fits the following advice about leaving them.
rows.anchor: والمعنى الثاني أن يعبر بالقيام عن انبعاثهم بالعزم إلى الهروب إلى الله

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-A'mash reads 'when they stood, standing, and said,' adding qiyāman.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش «إذ قاموا قياما فقالوا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shatatan means injustice, crossing a limit, or excess; the related verb describes overpricing and the root also conveys distance.
rows.anchor: والشطط الجور، وتعدي الحد والغلو بحسب الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths' statement about their people's gods could have been made before the king or among themselves as they prepared to leave.
rows.anchor: وقولهم: هؤلاء قومنا مقالة تصلح أن تكون مما قالوا في مقامهم بين يدي الملك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge 'why do they not bring proof' is an exhortation to do the impossible, thereby nullifying the people's claim; sultan means proof, while Qatada glosses it as a clear excuse.
rows.anchor: وقولهم: لولا يأتون تحضيض بمعنى التعجيز، لأنه تحضيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their rhetorical question that none is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God magnifies the guilt of those who invoke other gods.
rows.anchor: ثم عظموا جرم الداعين مع الله آلهة وظلمهم بقوله على جهة التقرير فمن أظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The advice in verse 16 is best read as what they said to one another when they resolved to leave; if verse 14 means an audience with the king, an omitted 'some said to others' is needed here.
rows.anchor: وبهذا يترجح أن قوله تعالى: إذ قاموا فقالوا إنما المراد به إذ عزموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the idolaters knew and revered God while associating idols with Him, 'except God' is a connected exception; if they knew only idols, it is disconnected.
rows.anchor: فهو استثناء منقطع ليس من الأول، وإن فرضناهم يعرفون الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Ibn Masud's wording 'what they worship besides God' explains the verse's phrase about what the people worship.
rows.anchor: الله» ، قال قتادة هذا تفسيرها

rows.speaker: هارون
rows.claim: Harun reports that some copies of Ibn Masud's codex read 'what they worship besides us.'
rows.anchor: قال هارون وفي بعض مصاحفه «وما يعبدون من دوننا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse pictures their mutual counsel: having separated from the unbelievers, they would take refuge in the cave and rely on God to spread mercy and provide ease; the prayer concerns worldly life.
rows.anchor: ومضمن هذه الآية أن بعضهم قال لبعض إذ فارقنا الكفار وانفردنا بالله تعالى فلنجعل الكهف مأوى

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir read marfiqan with an open mīm and kasra on fāʾ; Abu Zayd calls this a verbal noun like rifq.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر «مرفقا» بفتح الميم وكسر الفاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي والحسن وطلحة والأعمش وابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: These readers use the opposite vowels; both forms can mean ease or a bodily joint, though lexicographers disagree about which form denotes the joint.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي والحسن وطلحة والأعمش وابن أبي إسحاق «مرفقا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following verse, attributed in the preceding passage to an unnamed poet, illustrates shatata as going too far in reproach.
rows.anchor: ألا يا لقوم قد اشتط عواذلي ... ويزعمن أن أودى بحقي باطلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits the transition: they took refuge in the cave, God caused them to sleep, and they remained so.
rows.anchor: بين هاتين الآيتين اقتضاب يبينه ما تقدم من الآيات، تقديره فآووا

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers assimilate the initial tāʾ in tazāwar; other readings simplify or reshape the form, but all mean that the sun veers, turns, or inclines.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو «تزاور» بتشديد الزاي وإدغام التاء

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash explains tazāwar as turning away; zawr means inclination, as in an eye that looks askance, and poetry uses azwar for a slanted side.
rows.anchor: أما أن الأخفش قال «تزور» معناه تنتقض والزور الميل، والأزور في العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Rabi'a's verse uses azwar for a body's side turned away in fear.
rows.anchor: وجنبي خيفة القوم أزور ومن اللفظة قول عنترة: [الكامل]

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: Antara's line uses the verb izwarra for turning aside from a spear strike.
rows.anchor: ومن اللفظة قول عنترة: [الكامل] فازور من وقع القنا بلبانه

rows.speaker: بشر بن أبي حازم
rows.claim: Bishr ibn Abi Hazim's poem uses izwirar for a deviation in direction.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول بشر بن أبي حازم: [الوافر] تؤم بها الحداة مياه نخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report about the expedition of Mu'ta says the Prophet noticed Abdullah ibn Rawaha's bier slanting away from the biers of Ja'far and Zayd.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث غزوة مؤتة، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the feminine verb taqriḍuhum; a minority uses yaqriḍuhum, with the cave as subject, cutting them off from sunlight.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «تقرضهم» بالتاء، وفرقة «يقرضهم» بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the sun did not reach the sleepers at all; taqriḍuhum means that it left them untouched.
rows.anchor: وجمهور من قرأ بالتاء، فالمعنى أنهم كانوا لا تصيبهم شمس البتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group of readers who use taqriḍuhum says the afternoon sun reached them, benefiting their bodies while cutting them off from the rest of its path.
rows.anchor: قالوا كان في مسها لهم بالعشي صلاح لأجسامهم

rows.speaker: ذي الرمة
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's verse uses qarada for cutting across a place, supporting the sun's described course.
rows.anchor:
ومنه قول ذي الرمة: [الطويل]
إلى ظعن يقرضن أجواز مشرف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj and others say the cave faced the Pleiades; its upper part was sheltered from rain, while al-Zajjaj also treats the sun's behavior itself as a divine sign independent of the entrance's direction.
rows.anchor: حكى الزجاج وغيره قال: كان باب الكهف ينظر إلى بنات نعش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Right and left most naturally refer to the cave as if its entrance were a person's face; alternatively they can be measured relative to the sun's rays.
rows.anchor: والوجه الأول أصح و «الفجوة» المتسع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajwa means an open space; Qatada says open area and Ibn Jubayr says an inner place, with Prophetic usage also applying it to a gap in a route.
rows.anchor: و «الفجوة» المتسع وجمعها فجى، قال قتادة: في فضاء منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'that is among God's signs' points to the entire arrangement; on al-Zajjaj's view it singles out the sun's unusual course, followed by praise of God.
rows.anchor: وقوله ذلك من آيات الله الإشارة إلى الأمر بجملته، وعلى قول الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse narrates a past condition with present-tense verbs for vividness; ayqaz is the plural of yaqiz, an awake person.
rows.anchor: صفة حال قد نقضت وجاءت أفعالها مستقبلة تجوزا واتساعا وأيقاظا جمع يقظ

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Commentators say their eyes were open while they slept, making an observer think they were awake.
rows.anchor: قال أهل التفسير: كانت أعينهم مفتوحة وهم نائمون، فلذلك كان الرائي يحسبهم أيقاظا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author also suggests they seemed alert because they were carefully preserved and had not acquired the usual relaxed appearance of sleepers; open eyes would make this still clearer if reliably transmitted.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يحسب الرائي ذلك لشدة الحفظ الذي كان عليهم وقلة التغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author argues that the verse presents the turning as a separate report, not as the reason observers thought the youths were awake.
rows.anchor: فإن ألفاظ الآية لم تسقه إلا خبرا مستأنفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reports al-Hasan's alternate reading of the turning phrase, prefers Abu Hatim's syntax over Ibn Jinni's, and treats the turning as a separate reported action.
rows.anchor: فإن ألفاظ الآية لم تسقه إلا خبرا مستأنفا

rows.speaker: أبو عياض
rows.claim: Abu Iyad says the sleepers were turned over twice a year.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عياض: كان هذا التقليب مرتين في السنة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says they were turned once every seven years.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة كل سبع سنين مرة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group restricts the turning to the final nine years.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة إنما قلبوا في التسع الأواخر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the turning protected them from the ground, and sunlight would have burned them; without turning, earth would have consumed them.
rows.anchor: لو مستهم الشمس لأحرقتهم، ولولا التقليب لأكلتهم الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says avoiding feeding, sunlight, and contact with the ground through such a long sleep is more wondrous than simply preserving them from sun and earth; the reports are conjectural.
rows.anchor: وآية الله في نومهم هذه المدة الطويلة وحياتهم دون تغد أذهب في الغرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators generally attribute the turning to God's command and the angels; the author allows instead that God enabled the living youths to turn without waking.
rows.anchor: وظاهر كلام المفسرين أن التقليب كان بأمر الله وفعل ملائكته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators say the dog was real and belonged to a hunter among them; another account has a shepherd and his dog join the youths.
rows.anchor: أكثر المفسرين على أنه كلب حقيقة

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الجوهري
rows.claim: A preacher, as heard by Ibn Atiyya's father, said that loving virtuous people brings blessing, citing the dog remembered in the Qur'an because it accompanied good people.
rows.anchor: إن من أحب أهل الخير نال من بركتهم، كلب أحب أهل فضل وصحبهم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports unnamed views that the dog was a cook among the youths or one of the youths stationed as a lookout; the author says the human reading is weakened by the extended arms, a dog's familiar posture.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة كان رجلا طباخا لهم حكاه الطبري ولم يسم قائله

rows.speaker: أبو عمر المطرز
rows.claim: Abu Umar al-Muṭarriz reports a reading kalibahum, which may mean a human sentry lying low with arms extended or the dog itself.
rows.anchor: وقد حكى أبو عمر المطرز في كتاب اليواقيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle bāsit is used with past meaning because the verse depicts a scene; wasid means the cave threshold or its site, with courtyard, door, and ground also reported, and the author prefers threshold.
rows.anchor: اسم الفاعل وهو بمعنى المضي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير
rows.claim: They gloss wasid as a courtyard; Ibn Abbas also says door and Ibn Jubayr also says earth.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير «الوصيد» الفناء، وقال ابن عباس أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce law iṭṭalaʿta with kasra on wāw, while some use ḍamma; the lam in lamilʾta is geminated by one group to intensify the sense, but plain form is more common.
rows.anchor: وقرأ «لو اطلعت» بكسر الواو جمهور القراء، وقرأ الأعمش وابن وثاب

rows.speaker: المخبل السعدي
rows.claim: Al-Mukhabbal al-Saʿdi's verse attests the intensified form of the verb meaning to be filled.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء التثقيل في قول المخبل السعدي: [الطويل]

rows.speaker: المهدوي والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi and al-Zajjaj suggest their frightening hair and nails caused the terror, but the author calls this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة إنما حفهم هذا الرعب لطول شعورهم وأظفارهم، ذكره المهدوي والزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God preserved their sleeping appearance as a sign: their clothes and bodies did not change, while the awakened youth noticed only changes to the land and buildings.
rows.anchor: أن الله عز وجل حفظ لهم الحالة التي ناموا عليها

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim says both pronunciations of ruʿban, with a silent or rounded ʿayn, are valid dialect forms.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حاتم: هما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Likewise' points to God's preceding treatment of the youths; baʿth means setting something in motion after stillness, and the lam in 'so they might question one another' marks an outcome rather than their purpose.
rows.anchor: الإشارة بذلك إلى الأمر الذي ذكر الله في جهتهم، والعبرة التي فعلها فيهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about duration suggests that a speaker sensed their sleep had exceeded ordinary limits; they seem to have awakened under similar time and weather conditions, since an abrupt change would be unlikely.
rows.anchor: وقول القائل كم لبثتم يقتضي أنه هجس في خاطره طول نومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary between warq with kasra or sukūn on rāʾ; other reported forms change the vowels or assimilate consonants, while Ali reads bawāriq, a collective noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Narratives say they awoke hungry and sent Tamlikha to buy food after praying as though only one night had passed; the cave entrance may have collapsed or a shepherd may have opened it.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنهم انتبهوا جياعا، وأن المبعوث هو تلميخا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the extended story, Tamlikha put on shabby clothes, found the city and its landmarks changed, saw signs of the Christian faith, and feared that he had lost his mind.
rows.anchor: فأخذ تلميخا ثيابا رثة منكرة ولبسها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He tried to buy food with an old coin; the seller and townspeople recognized it as money from an ancient king and questioned him about a hidden treasure.
rows.anchor: فدفع إليه دراهم كأخفاف الربع فيما ذكر، فعجب لها البياع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer king Bedousis heard Tamlikha's story, linked him to the youths recorded on a copper tablet, and went with the people to the cave; the youths either emerged and honored the king or, in the more common account, died after Tamlikha told them the city was Muslim.
rows.anchor: هذا مجنون، اذهبوا به إلى الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says he has shortened the many conflicting versions, retaining the details needed to explain the verse and relying on what he considers sounder.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا القصص من اختلاف الروايات والألفاظ ما تضيق به الصحف، فاختصرته،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths' use of an agent to buy food establishes the validity of agency; Ali appointed his brother Aqil to act for him in Uthman's presence.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه البعثة بالورق الوكالة وصحتها،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Most readers use a silent lām in the command falyanzur; al-Hasan pronounces it with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «فلينظر» بسكون لام الأمر، وقرأ الحسن «فلينظر» بكسرها

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima glosses azka as greater in quantity; Qatada says better, Muqatil says more pleasant, and Ibn Jubayr says lawful, especially in view of food slaughtered by unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وأزكى معناه أكثر فيما ذكر عكرمة، وقال قتادة معناه خير، وقال مقاتل: المراد أطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains the lawful interpretation in light of food slaughtered by unbelievers; the youths are reported to have sought raisins, or dates in another account.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جبير: المراد أحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Liyatalattaf means to act discreetly and carefully; al-Hasan reads the lām with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقوله وليتلطف أي في اختفائه وتحيله، وقرأ الحسن «وليتلطف» بكسر اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'if they discover you' refers to the unbelievers, followers of Daqiyus; yathharu means they overcome or capture you.
rows.anchor: والضمير في إنهم عائد على الكفار

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains rajm as stoning with rocks.
rows.anchor: وقولهم يرجموكم قال الزجاج معناه بالحجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author considers stoning the stronger sense: the king meant to kill them if he caught them, and stoning was a customary punishment for those opposing a community's religion.
rows.anchor: وهو الأصح، لأنه كان عازما على قتلهم لو ظفر بهم

rows.speaker: حجاج
rows.claim: Hajjaj instead interprets yarjumukum as verbal abuse.
rows.anchor: وقال حجاج، يرجموكم معناه بالقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Likewise' links discovering the youths to the prior awakening; athara is the causative of stumbling on something, a metaphor for discovering concealed knowledge.
rows.anchor: الإشارة بذلك في قوله وكذلك إلى بعثناهم ليتسائلوا [الكهف: 19]

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says 'so that they might know' refers to the Muslim community of the youths' era, which had fallen into dispute over bodily resurrection; God revealed the sleepers, convincing doubters and consoling a distressed king.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب الطبري، وذلك أنهم، فيما روي، دخلتهم حينئذ فتنة في أمر الحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Tabari's reading, the king was so troubled by people's doubt that he wore rough garments, sat in ashes, and prayed for proof until the youths were discovered.
rows.anchor: فشق على ملكهم ذلك وبقي حيران لا يدري كيف يبين أمره لهم، حتى لبس المسوح وقعد على الرماد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, 'so that they might know' refers to the youths themselves, whose story became a sign of bodily resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي جعل الله أمرهم آية لهم دالة على بعث الأجساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'the Hour has no doubt in it' asserts that the Hour is objectively certain even though people may doubt it.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن الساعة في نفسها وحقيقتها لا شك فيها، وإن كان الشك قد وقع لناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A separate disagreement concerns whether to cover the cave or build over it; some said the youths were dead and others alive, and a dominant party proposed a mosque. Qatada identifies that party as the rulers.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن التنازع إنما هو في أن اطلعوا عليهم فقال بعض هم أموات، وبعض هم أحياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says believers who wanted the cave obscured prevailed over those who insisted on construction, and made the required building a mosque.
rows.anchor: فلما غلبت الأولى على أن يكون بنيان ولا بد، قالت يكون مسجدا، فكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says unbelievers wanted a church or pagan shrine, but believers resisted and insisted on a mosque.
rows.anchor: وروي أن الطائفة التي دعت إلى البنيان

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says God concealed the youths' trace from people, prompting construction of a building to mark their location.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عبيد بن عمير أن الله عمى على الناس حينئذ أثرهم، وحجبهم عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun 'they will say' refers to contemporary People of the Torah, who disagreed about the number of sleepers.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قوله سيقولون يراد به أهل التوراة، من معاصري محمد

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin reads thalath with the tāʾ assimilated into thāʾ; other readers vary the vowels of khamsa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «ثلاثة» ، وقرأ ابن محيصن «ثلاث»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajman bil-ghayb means conjecture, pictured as repeatedly throwing guesses at an unknown target; the word is associated with tarjuman and the translating of a book.
rows.anchor: وقوله رجما بالغيب معناه ظنا، وهو مستعار من الرجم

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr's line calls speech about war without direct knowledge hadithan murajjaman, a conjectural report.
rows.anchor:
ومنه قول زهير: [الطويل]
وما الحرب إلا ما علمتم وذقتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw before 'and their eighth' is ordinary conjunction separating the final report and could be omitted; the author rejects a special 'waw of eight' rule.
rows.anchor: والواو في قوله وثامنهم طريق النحويين فيها أنها واو عطف دخلت في آخر إخبار عن عددهم

rows.speaker: ابن خالويه
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh and others call it the 'waw of eight'; al-Thaʿlabi reports Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash's claim that Quraysh inserted a waw in a sequence naming eight.
rows.anchor: وتقول فرقة منها ابن خالويه: هي واو الثمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says examples sometimes offered for the 'waw of eight' are either wrongly analyzed or require the conjunction grammatically, as in the verses about seven nights and eight days.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله تعالى: ثيبات وأبكارا [التحريم: 5]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to return knowledge of their number to God; only a few among the People of the Book know, and Ibn Abbas says he is among them and that there were seven plus the dog.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن عباس يقول: أنا من ذلك القليل، وكانوا سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seven is supported because the first two reported counts are explicitly called conjecture, while the seven-and-eighth report is left unchallenged; the conjunction also suits a correct count of eight.
rows.anchor: بأن القرآن لما حكى قول من قال «ثلاثة وخمسة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of 'a manifest argument' is to rely on what revelation makes clear and return knowledge of the number to God; another is simply to tell them they are wrong without probing hidden details.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: فلا تمار فيهم إلا مراء ظاهرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word may also mean 'departing,' supported by a poetic line; al-Tabrizi is credited with this reading at the preceding segment boundary.
rows.anchor:
ظاهرا معناه ذاهبا، وأنشد:
وتلك شكاة ظاهر عنك عارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not license pointless disputation: the term 'argument' is figurative for replying to People of the Book with an outward statement, unlike blameworthy hidden disputation; miraʾ derives from doubt.
rows.anchor: ولم يبح له في هذه الآية أن يماري، ولكن قوله إلا مراء استعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun 'about them' refers to the sleepers, while 'from them' means the contemporary People of the Book; 'their number' is omitted but understood.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله فيهم عائد على أهل الكهف، وفي قوله منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reproached the Prophet for promising to answer the unbelievers' questions the next day without saying 'if God wills'; revelation was delayed fifteen days, distressing him and prompting rumors, until these verses brought relief.
rows.anchor: عاتب الله تعالى فيها نبيه عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction is to condition plans for the future on God's will; the lam in 'for a thing' can mean 'in' or 'about'.
rows.anchor: وأمر في هذه الآية أن يقول في أمر من الأمور: إني أفعل غدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'except if God wills' has an implied command to say 'if God wills'; it directs mention of God's will rather than serving as an exception from the prohibition.
rows.anchor: تقديره: إلا أن تقول إلا أن يشاء الله، أو إلا أن تقول إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports and rejects the reading that 'except if God wills' is an exception to the prohibition itself; the author says it is so unsound that it should not have been cited.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول حكاه الطبري ورد عليه،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan say 'remember your Lord when you forget' means to say the exception later if you forgot it initially, joining those who condition their plans on God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والحسن معناه، والإشارة به إلى الاستثناء

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima interprets 'when you forget' as 'when you become angry.'
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: المعنى واذكر ربك إذا غضبت

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Although the verse concerns the general practice of saying 'if God wills,' Malik and many jurists say an oath's exception only works and cancels expiation when joined to the oath.
rows.anchor: أما مالك رحمه الله وجميع أصحابه، فيما علمت، وكثير من العلماء،

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata allows an oath's exception up to the time needed to milk a large-yield camel.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء له أن يستثني في قدر حلب الناقة الغزيرة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada allows the exception before the oath is spoken.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة إن استثنى قبل أن يقول أو يتكلم فله ثنياه

rows.speaker: ابن حنبل وابن راهويه
rows.claim: Ibn Hanbal and Ibn Rahawayh allow the exception while the person is still engaged in the matter.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن حنبل له الاستثناء ما دام في ذلك الأمر، وقاله ابن راهويه

rows.speaker: طاوس والحسن
rows.claim: Tawus and al-Hasan allow it while the oath-taker remains in the same sitting.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول حكاه الطبري ورد عليه،

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr allows a delayed exception for up to four months.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير ينفع الاستثناء بعد أربعة أشهر فقط

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to allow a delayed exception even after a year; Mujahid says two years and Abu al-Aliya says indefinitely.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ينفع الاستثناء ولو بعد سنة، وقال مجاهد بعد سنتين،

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari interprets Ibn Abbas as meaning that a person may later join the category of those who remember to qualify their plans, not that expiation disappears; a Prophetic report requires expiation when one chooses a better course after an oath.
rows.anchor: إنما أراد ابن عباس أنه ينفع في أن يحصل الحالف في رتبة المستثنين بعد سنة من حلفه

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawi says Ibn Abbas discussed a future promise, not an oath whose bond one wants to dissolve.
rows.anchor: إنما تكلم ابن عباس في أن الاستثناء بعد سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some jurists attribute to Ibn Abbas the view that a delayed exception cancels expiation, and infer the same for anyone who says a delayed exception is valid.
rows.anchor: وذهبت فرقة من الفقهاء إلى أن مذهب ابن عباس سقوط الكفارة وألزموا كل من يقول ينفع الاستثناء بعد مدة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik and others limit an exception to an oath by God, excluding divorce and vows to travel to Mecca; al-Shafiʿi, jurists of opinion, Tawus, and Hammad allow exceptions in those other commitments too.
rows.anchor: وليس الاستثناء إلا في اليمين بالله، لا يكون في طلاق ونحوه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verbal exception does not help with a deliberately false oath; an exception must itself be spoken aloud.
rows.anchor: وليس في اليمين الغموس استثناء ينفع، ولا يكون الاستثناء بالقول،

rows.speaker: محمد الكوفي المفسر
rows.claim: Muhammad al-Kufi says the words 'perhaps my Lord will guide me' are a required formula and expiation for anyone who forgot the exception.
rows.anchor: قال محمد الكوفي المفسر: إنها بألفاظها مما أمر أن يقولها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most interpreters treat the phrase as a general supplication, not a formula restricted to making up a forgotten exception.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور هو دعاء مأمور به دون هذا التخصيص

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the prayer asks God to make a nearer sign of the Prophet's mission clear than the story of the sleepers.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج المعنى عسى أن ييسر الله من الأدلة على نبوتي أقرب من دليل أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the broader sense: may God guide the Prophet more rightly in future affairs; although addressed to him, the instruction extends to the community because people often need it.
rows.anchor: وما قدمته أصوب، أي عسى أن يرشدني فيما استقبل

rows.speaker: قتادة ومطر الوراق
rows.claim: Qatada and Matar al-Warraq say the statement about three hundred years is a quotation of what the Israelites said, citing Ibn Masud's codex wording 'and they said'; Qatada takes that phrase as attached to the earlier reported claims.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة ومطر الوراق وغيرهما ولبثوا في كهفهم الآية حكاية عن بني إسرائيل أنهم قالوا ذلك

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari records an objection that if the duration were God's own report, the command 'say: God knows best' would be pointless.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: وقال بعضهم: لو كان ذلك خبرا من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that objection: God reports the true duration, then tells Muhammad to answer disputants that God's knowledge settles their disagreement.
rows.anchor: وما الوجه المفهوم البارع إلا أن تكون الآية خبرا عن لبثهم،

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The verifying scholars hold that God states how long they slept, then 'God knows best how long they stayed' refers to later disputed events.
rows.anchor: وقال المحققون: بل قوله تعالى: ولبثوا في كهفهم الآية

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says the Israelites disputed how long the youths remained after discovery; three hundred and nine years describes their sleep, while the later period, from their death until Muhammad's time and disappearance, was unknown.
rows.anchor: فأخبر الله نبيه أن هذه المدة في كونهم نياما، وأن ما بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says people disputed what units the additional nine represented—hours, days, weeks, months, or years—so God directed them to return the question to Him; ordinary Arabic implies years.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضها إنه لما قال: وازدادوا تسعا لم يدر الناس أهي ساعات

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash explains the nine-year difference as converting three hundred solar years into the equivalent lunar count used by the Arab audience.
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش ما معناه: أنهم لبثوا ثلاثمائة سنة شمسية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They apparently entered the cave shortly after Jesus, while some of his disciples were still alive.
rows.anchor: والظاهر من أمرهم أنهم قاموا ودخلوا الكهف بعد عيسى بيسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers put tanwin on miʾa and treat sinin as a substitute, explanatory apposition, or specification; Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Yahya, Talha, and al-Aʿmash attach miʾa to sinin without tanwin.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «ثلاثمائة سنين» بتنوين مائة ونصب «سنين»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The continuation gives Ibn Masud's codex reading as 'three hundred years'; al-Dahhak has a plural reading and Abu Amr a vowel variant.
rows.anchor: «ثلاثمائة سنة» ، وقرأ الضحاك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada takes 'how seeing and hearing He is' as an exclamation: no one sees or hears more fully than God.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لا أحد أبصر من الله ولا أسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, God sees by His revelation and guidance and lets the Prophet see proofs and truth; the two verbs may express two distinct ideas rather than an exclamation.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المعنى: أبصر به أي بوحيه وإرشاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'they have no protector' may refer to the sleepers, whom no one besides God guarded, or to the Prophet's unbelieving opponents, as a threat.
rows.anchor: ما لهم من دونه من ولي يحتمل أن يعود الضمير في لهم على أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the indicative 'and He does not associate anyone in His judgment'; Ibn Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Raja, Qatada, and al-Jahdari read it as a prohibition addressed to the Prophet, while Mujahid has a jussive reading whose grammar Yaqub cannot explain.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «ولا يشرك في حكمه أحدا» بالياء من تحت

rows.speaker: الضحاك بن مزاحم
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says people first asked whether the three hundred meant months, days, or years, after which the words 'years and nine more' were revealed.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن الضحاك بن مزاحم أنه قال: نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: On a Syrian campaign Ibn Abbas saw bones at a cave and said the sleepers had perished long ago; a monk was surprised that an Arab knew this.
rows.anchor: فروي عن ابن عباس أنه مر بالشام في بعض غزواته، مع ناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another tradition says the Prophet foretold that Jesus would make the pilgrimage with the sleepers, who had not yet made it.
rows.anchor: وروت فرقة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: قال ليحجن عيسى ابن مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many people in Syria identify a cave with corpses, a mosque, a structure called al-Raqim, and a dog skeleton as the sleepers' site; Ibn Atiyya says he also visited the reported cave near Loja in Granada in 504 AH and saw corpses and a dog remains, nearby Roman ruins and a site called Daqiyus.
rows.anchor: وبالأندلس في جهة غرناطة بقرب قرية تسمى لوشة، كهف فيه موتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He records these claimed sites because their enduring marvel is worth remembering, though earlier generations left no reliable indication of their identity.
rows.anchor: وإنما استسهلت ذكر هذا مع بعده لأنه عجب يتخلد ذكره ما شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the previous reading is a prohibition against associating partners, 'recite' continues it; if it is an indicative statement, this verse begins a new command.
rows.anchor: من قرأ «ولا تشرك» بالنهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command may continue the reproach over forgetting the exception: answer the questions by reciting God's revelation, follow it in practice, and recount what was revealed.
rows.anchor: كأنه يقول هذه أجوبة الأسئلة فاتل وحي الله إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Multahad means a refuge or side to lean toward; lahd names the slant in one side of a grave, and ilhad is deviation from truth.
rows.anchor: و «الملتحد» : الجانب الذي يمال إليه، ومعنى اللحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'None can alter His words' does not deny abrogation: it either means no one but God can alter them or refers to reports and other words not subject to abrogation; the unchanging speech is God's attribute governing destiny, while Ibn Abbas says revealed books change only through interpretation.
rows.anchor: ولا يفسر قوله لا مبدل لكلماته أمر النسخ لأن المعنى:
